body_markdown:
A little over two months ago, I watched a 1998 Mitsubishi Montero pull out of my driveway and head down the road, until it disappeared. The[old-school Japanese SUV](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/montero-in-moab-growing-to-love-an-overlooked-4x4-in-the-age-of-escape/) had been mine for five years, serving as a daily driver, an adventure rig, a winter warrior, and a constantly charming vehicle that forced me to slow down, be more deliberate, and get my hands dirty on countless occasions.


As it pulled away, I turned back to my garage and saw a few things: first, my wife’s car, a wonderful 2013 Toyota Highlander Limited, of which I cannot say enough good things. Second, several toolboxes, a snowblower, some industrial shelves, a cabinet, and plenty of tools and materials (but also nowhere near enough) to tackle automotive and home projects of all sorts.


With its tall rooftop tent, the Montero never actually lived in the garage, but I still considered it a crucial part of “my garage.” It was “the fun vehicle.” Now it’s all business: We have the Highlander and a 2016 GMC Sierra 1500, my new daily driver.


There is no “fun” vehicle at my house anymore. “The garage” is empty.


Lisa Anna | Unsplash


That has left me with mixed feelings. Without a doubt, my life is busy with right now trying to hold down the fort at home, keeping my beautiful baby daughter alive, and remaining a valuable member of society—not to mention a halfway decent husband. I’m at a stage where I need my vehicles to just flat-out *work* every time I crank the starter.


But yes, there are times when I feel like a failed enthusiast because of it. The twinge hits me when a friend or colleague scoops a new fun ride, or when I see a listing on Facebook Marketplace that I *technically* could swing but know I shouldn’t. Maybe you’ve been there before, or know someone who has. This hobby is rarely cheap, and it’s understandable to feel sheepish when answering the question, “So, what do you drive?” with something ordinary—or with no answer at all.


Not my garage. But space means possibility and potential.


Point3d Commercial Imaging Ltd. | Unsplash


After some late-night consideration while rocking my daughter to sleep, though, I’m starting to view this situation differently. Having an empty garage and still choosing to chase this hobby simply makes you a *different* kind of enthusiast. A gearhead with a joyless keyring, who chooses to spend their precious free time engaging with the hobby anyway? That’s unobligated devotion. We should celebrate those folks, not scorn them when they show up empty-handed to a Sunday morning cruise.


There are plenty of ways to practice passion for cars. For me, right now, it’s more focused maintenance on the daily drivers. With each brake job or[oil change](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/8-oil-change-dos-and-donts/) , I try to come away with a little more knowledge for next time or—hopefully only rarely—a good “don’t make that mistake again” moment (which is still more[knowledge for next time](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/6-diy-lessons-we-all-learn-eventually/) ). In trying to maintain my cars, I’ve found myself poking down YouTube wormholes to learn about fuses, HVAC systems, metallurgy, and plenty of other topics directly or tangentially related to “the hobby.” Right now, that stuff helps me keep my half-ton pickup on the road, but maybe someday it will help spur along the restoration of an old ’80s pickup.


That’s me, on the right. A full garage is more fun, to be sure.


[Jordan Lewis](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/jlewishagerty-com/)


Other times, I’ll take a quick jaunt over to a friend’s house to help them with one of their projects. Even if it’s just holding the flashlight, it’s a chance to be around the labor of love that keeps these machines on the road, when more timid souls have long since given up. There’s an osmosis by proximity here that usually sees me leave the shop smarter or more motivated than when I showed up. Stack the little wins one at a time, if you have to.


Kayla Keenan


Beyond just helping out in a friend’s garage, the same good feelings emerge when I drop by Cars and Caffeine at the Hagerty headquarters on Friday mornings during the summer. Like clockwork, showing up yields chances to tap into enthusiast energy, the kind that that courses through the veins of those who opt for a cup of joe and a sunrise rather than a few more hours of sleep. The same can be said for the racetrack, when I’m fortunate enough to get out to one.


If there aren’t any brakes to be swapped or burned fuses to chase, sometimes, encouraging my inner enthusiast is as simple as popping open a car magazine—we happen to make an[exceptional one](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine/) —and reading a story that invites me to envision myself behind the wheel. Other times it’s a social media scroll, (often too late at night). Even if I have no emotional tie to the car or people, I just want to see what others are doing, how they’re struggling through adversity, and hopefully learning something.


Those of you who do have a fun car in the garage should share it with the world as much as you can. You have the vessel for passion that others come out to see and follow on social media. To you, I tip a greasy ball cap. But on the off-chance you know a person who pines for a fun car, I’d offer this suggestion: Invite them over to wrench or just to idly poke at a neat machine. Maybe you see in them the same dreamer you once were.


And for those in my camp, it doesn’t have to be forever. Circumstances evolve. Dreaming is free.
